en: Must have given my child their teat.
The patrons who accompanied my Manas
Must all have come together to this orphan.
O Kanykei, by Baabedin,
My foal, God has granted your wish!
O Kanykei, my foal,
If your orphan lives long,
His right shoulder will be broad,
His twelve limbs well proportioned.
Like Manas, gone to the other world,
This child will be a lion like his father.
He will be a blaze of glowing embers;
The enemy he charges will be stopped.
He will set grassy land afire.
If he survives, Semetey
Will kindle the feather-grass plains,
Will pour blood into the running water.
When he returns, he will lead a migration.
Put aside your grief, Kanykei.
When he returns to Talas,
You will see him avenge himself on the six villains!
If God lets him see the Kyrgyz,
O Kanykei, my foal,
He will fulfill your wish.
When he grows enraged,
He will have men's heads cut off.
Those who understand his words
He will bring to obedience by words;
To a fool who will not understand,
He will show that he is a lion.
When his anger is roused,
He will chase white deer and make them cattle.
If my orphan takes after his father,
He will throw the whole world into turmoil.
This orphan left you by the gray-maned hero
Will herd gray deer and make them cattle.
If he grows safely without dying,
He will throw every land he sees into turmoil.
O Kanykei, do not grieve:
God has granted your wish.
Manas, gone to the Last Judgment,
Had a dervish companion.
As I lay at night, I saw
He had come to your child's cradle.
Saying, ‘The orphan left by Manas,’
He had offered your orphan his hand.
The one clasping his hand
Was the naked old man Kydyr.
To tell the child
He had words of counsel.
Standing there that night, the dervish
Said this to Semetey:
‘Do not shrink from an enemy exchanging shots.
Death is in God's hands;
Do not retreat from an enemy you meet.
Until you reach twelve,
You will be in the city of Bukhara.
When your age reaches twelve,
You will return to your village.
May all your fortunes prosper;
My foal, become a greater lion than your father!’
The dervish gave his blessing;
I saw him set things right.
That gray-maned king Manas—
I saw how he protected him.
I saw Baabedin of the road
Grant the orphan passage.
All the lions blessed by Kydyr,
Raising a shout,
I saw grant the orphan passage.
Calling him the pennant fastened to the spear,
To your father Temir's city
Let us wander, carrying him on our backs.
Calling him the gift left by the Magnanimous One,
The hoof left by the winged steed,
Let us present him as a fitting gift,
The lamp left by the falcon.
O Kanykei, my foal,
Grieving is of no use:
Your gray-maned Manas will not return.
Lamenting offers no remedy;
What is seen today is gone tomorrow.
O Kanykei, my foal,
Such is this shitty world!
Put aside your pride and shame,
O Kanykei, my foal:
Your magnanimous Manas is not here!
Traveling forty days without rest,
My child, let us settle as wanderers in Bukhara.
Until your orphan reaches twelve,
Do not cling to pride without cause.
Let us bear the name of wanderers!
Helplessly we fled from Talas.
You have indeed been parted, you see,
From your equal, Sultan Manas.
My foal, my child Kanykei,
You rose to rule from your youth.
A fugitive cannot stand defiant;
My foal, put that defiance from your mind.
When you stand defiant,
My child, your nobility is beyond reproach,
But those who sliced horse-belly fat and served tea,
Who freely served their food,
Who never had their fill when asking to eat,
Who never gave up their greed,
Who, driven into the darkness,
Prowled like leopards—
Kanykei, my child, your noble Kyrgyz people are not here!
When we reach your father Karakan,
Let us behave as fugitives;
Do not stand defiant without cause!
Until Semetey reaches twelve,
If they say, ‘Make your home with the Sarts,’
Let us stay among them.
O Kanykei, my foal,
Until your orphan reaches twelve,
In that city of Bukhara
Let us meekly bend to our lot.
Kanykei, let us leave our former ways.
My foal, until your orphan mounts a horse,
Let us begin a different manner of life.
If you care to listen, Kanykei,
Revered Chyiyrdy
Has words she wishes to say.
Ahead lie Alty-Shaar, Kokand and Margalan;
Your gray-maned hero humiliated them,
And these people hold a grudge.
Abandon such haughty speech!
Until your orphan matures and mounts a horse,
O Kanykei, my foal,
Abandon your haughty speech!
O Kanykei, my foal,
Begin with gentle words!
When her husband dies, a woman
Comes to rest in an ill-suited place.
When a wife loses her khan,
When her husband dies, to a woman
Her birth family is nearest.
O my cherished Kanykei,
This is my counsel, these are my words,
My revered foal;
These are your mother's sorrowful words.”
Hearing this, Kanykei
Prayed to God.
Putting aside their former thoughts,
“Amen!” said the two ladies.
The joint of meat left from the two-year-old wether
They dedicated to Baabedin and ate their fill.
The two ladies gained strength,
Coughing harshly again and again.
Was he not left by their khan?
That cradle-infant Semetey
They took turns carrying,
And over the saddle of Aman-Jol
The two ladies went.
Setting their faces toward Bukhara,
Carrying Semetey,
The two ladies fled.
To Temir Khan's city
The two ladies wandered.
There was cradle-infant Semetey;
There went Kanykei in mourning;
There went Semetey in flight!
In some places, for two days
They went on without staying.
On the face of this earth, the bereft
Went on, finding no room.
Over ridge after curving ridge
They kept crossing;
Toward Bukhara the two ladies
Kept fleeing.
Many a sloping pass
They crossed on foot.
By day they walked without rest,
By night they fled in desperate haste;
In the wild, spirit-haunted plain
The two ladies fled alone.
Then your uncle Bakai,
Your wise and mighty falcon,
That dear one unlike other men,
Your old Bakai, never resting,
The torments of this world—
Your saint knew them in full.
When his friend Manas was alive,
Had been a well-built fortress.
That uncle Bakai
Had been a renowned khan.
Against that uncle Bakai
No one had dared cause trouble.
In all this vast world,
None remained to raise a catching-pole against Bakai.
In former days, when they lived in Talas,
Manas and Bakai had risen as khans;
At news of them, souls fled bodies.
The heroes turned like lions.
When he heard their great and famous renown,
Karakan, khan of the khakans,
Heard it and his heart grew narrow.
His wrath had spread through the world,
But when the khan of Beijing heard,
He fell into utter turmoil.
The father of so many people,
Your magnanimous Manas had died.
For the orphan left behind,
The hero Bakai suffered anguish.
“A spring in the winding mountains,” he thought,
“The little one left by my friend.
Without boots, wearing stockings,
Has Kanykei perhaps died?
She has no milk to drink for food,
Nor a horse to ride to Bukhara.
Perhaps disease struck her ribs,
Perhaps she coughed and died,” he thought.
“Or did one person, carrying two lives,
My precious child Kanykei,
Die from carrying them?” he thought.
“Her flanks sunken, her flesh wasted,
Did she fall ill and die?” he thought.
“My noble child Kanykei,
Fleeing to Bukhara,
Did she die from sores?” he thought.
“The sun is so hot that owls do not fly;
It is a terrible waterless desert.
Crushed by being carried along,
Meeting many sicknesses,
Semetey, left by the gray-maned hero—
Has he become exhausted and breathless?” he thought.
“Ill-willed Kanykei,
Fleeing on foot to Bukhara,
Without sleeping upon her elbow,
Without even a moment's rest,
My child Kanykei, unable to go on,
Has she worn herself out?” he thought.
“Alty-Shaar and the khan of Kokand,
Margalan below,
Samarkand above—
They had many raiding warriors.
Has my child met them and died?” he thought.
“Meeting them and performing deeds of valor,
Has my child died in a frenzy?” he thought.
Your uncle, the leopard Bakai,
Unable to remain still for grief,
Taking a palm-sized letter
About the distant widow,
About Semetey, left by his friend,
Had taken two well-fed horses,
Made his purpose known,
Saying, “I shall sacrifice to Baabedin;
I shall set my children on their road.”
He was carrying before him on the saddle
That two-year-old wether of Bolokbai's.
Alas, so many worries would not fit inside his breast.
“The orphan left me by the gray-maned hero
Will vanish from sight,” he thought;
Bakai's tears streamed in every direction.
In the sky Allah's sun grew clouded;
